accuracy.evidence: Checked against the National Curriculum English programmes of study Year 1 word reading (read common exception words, noting unusual correspondences between spelling and sound and where these occur in the word) and Appendix 1 exception word lists (the, said, was, you, they, of, come), Common Core RF.K.3c and RF.1.3g, and Ehri's account of orthographic mapping. Every grapheme claim was rechecked in standard southern British pronunciation: ai in said says /e/, a in was says /o/, ou in you says /oo/, e in the is a schwa, ey in they says /ai/, f in of says /v/; and, it, can and big are fully decodable.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips: thinking said rhymes with paid (prediction, then the ai tile is marked as the tricky part), confusing was and saw by reading the letters out of order (flash step distractor and prediction 'Yes, same letters'), spelling a tricky word as it sounds (sed, wos, waz and thay traps in the tile builder with their own corrections), and believing every high-frequency word is irregular so phonics is dropped (prediction on and, plus the sort where and, it, can and big go to Sound it out).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagsight is built around the exception-word mechanism itself: grapheme tiles with one irregular correspondence marked with a heart, a timed flash that tests instant recognition, ordered letter building with sound-alike traps, finding target words in connected sentences, and a decodable versus tricky sort. flagabc is letter names and shapes, flagjoin is handwriting joins, flagkinds is sentence types; none models grapheme-phoneme regularity or automaticity. The shingle gate passed against every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child finds that most of said sounds out and only ai does not, before the text says to learn the tricky part by heart; the flashed word hides after 1.2 s, so only recognition at a glance works; the builder refuses e after s in said and explains why, so the spelling of the irregular grapheme is learned by doing; the sentences show the same words in real text; the sort makes the child test each word by sounding it out.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: 'Yes, like paid' for said (the ai tile is shown to say e), 'Yes, same letters' for was and saw (the flash step treats them as different words), and 'Yes, all sight words are tricky' for and (the sort accepts and only under Sound it out). The done message quotes the child's guess through A.reveal.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating challenge questions with tagged wrong answers, each with its own correction: s and d (they say their usual sounds; the ai is tricky), saw (starts with s), wish (read each letter), sed (the tricky part is written ai), sad (s-a-d is a different word), trick (a-n-d sounds out), guess (no need to guess), pic (the picture cannot tell you the), skip (practise it). Lab mistakes name the slip too, for example 'It sounds like thay, but we write ey at the end.'

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short read-aloud sentences ('The s says s. The d says d.') and pass the family kid limit in validate_lessons; the adult text stays inside the family adult limit while using the precise phonics terms: common exception words, unusual correspondences between spelling and sound, high-frequency words, tricky words, grapheme-phoneme correspondence (GPC), irregular grapheme, decodable, orthographic mapping and automaticity.

no_filler.evidence: The filler gate passed. Each kid paragraph teaches one idea with a real word (said, was and saw, and, it and can); the adult paragraphs give the curriculum statements, how sight words are stored, four named teaching mistakes with a pace guide, and the lab outline. Explanation overlap with Knowing all letters, Syllables and the other phonics lessons stays under the 12 percent limit.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at iPhone 13 (390 px) in light and dark: the grapheme tiles for said are about 100 px wide with 34 px letters, the flash card and three choice tiles fit across, the letter builder shows four slots and five tiles in one row, the sentence words wrap onto two rows of tappable chips, and the sort bins are about 150 px wide. Buttons below repeat every target. Nothing is clipped.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs: axe reported no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light or dark on desktop and iPhone 13, no console or page errors, and every Show me completed. Every canvas tap or drag has a button twin (one per grapheme, per flash choice, per letter tile, per sentence word, and Sound it out and Tricky part), and the canvas aria-label speaks each change, for example 'Yes! In said, ai says e here, like in bed.'
